messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh is a 77-year-old Vietnamese American surgeon, married for over fifty years, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 56 following his witnessing of a catastrophic fire that broke out in the hospital wing where he was working. Several months ago, during a late surgical shift, a flash fire ignited in an adjacent ward. Minh did not escape the building immediately; instead, he moved toward the flames to help evacuate patients who could not move themselves. He watched a colleague become engulfed. The smell of burning — of cloth, of flesh — saturated the corridor. The heat pressed against his skin with an almost physical weight, and the sound of the fire alarm, shrill and irregular, cut through everything. He got out. His colleague did not. In the weeks that followed, what had seemed like the controlled competence of a lifetime in surgery began to fracture quietly and then loudly.

The memories that formed in the aftermath of that night are not memories in any ordinary sense. Minh describes them as disordered and strange — he cannot place the sequence of events in any reliable order, cannot say with certainty what came before what, and sometimes the emotional force of the event arrives without any accompanying image at all, a sudden crush of grief and terror that has no face. Most disorienting to him is the sense that the memory belongs to someone else, that the man in that corridor was not quite him — a dissociative quality that, rather than offering relief, deepens his conviction that something is fundamentally wrong with him as a person. He has come to believe that a surgeon of his experience and temperament should not be undone like this, and the memory's alien quality reads to him not as a natural response to horror but as evidence of a defective self. This appraisal — that he is broken in some essential way — pushes him toward the memory's edges rather than through it, and so the memory remains fragmented, its sequence unresolved, because every approach to it is also a retreat.

The fragmented and emotionally unpredictable nature of the memory keeps him in a state of chronic readiness. He is easily startled — a door closing in the hospital corridor will bring him upright, heart hammering — and he monitors ambient sounds with an attention that exhausts him. He is on high alert for anything sudden or loud, scanning his environment in the operating theatre, in the hallways, at home. This vigilance, which he experiences as necessary and rational given what he now believes about the world's unpredictability, is itself a form of re-exposure: the scanning keeps the threat architecture active, and in that heightened state, the sensory residue of the fire becomes easier to reach. A specific warmth against his skin — the ambient heat of a busy surgical suite, or simply a warm afternoon — can return him instantly to the corridor, and the smell of anything burnt, even toast in the hospital cafeteria, collapses the distance between then and now entirely. Stress, too — the ordinary stress of a complex case — functions as a trigger, flooding him with the same physiological urgency he felt that night.

When the triggers fire, Minh's response is to clamp down. He pushes away whatever is arising — thought, image, feeling — with a deliberate internal force, and he has stopped watching television or reading news that might carry stories of fires or disasters. He has also, more quietly, begun to push away positive emotions, moments of satisfaction after a successful procedure or warmth with his wife, because those feelings seem to him unsafe, as though allowing them would lower his guard. Yet the suppression does not clear the ground; it keeps the material pressurised and close, so that the triggers he is trying to avoid remain potent, and the fragmented memory stays unprocessed and available to intrude. His conviction that he must stay vigilant because anything can happen at any moment — a belief the fire confirmed for him — sustains the same hyperalert state that makes suppression feel necessary, and so the loop holds.

Concretely, Minh has begun declining complex elective cases, citing scheduling. His colleagues have noticed. His wife has noticed the silence at dinner. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in the scrub room when the warm water running over his hands stopped feeling like water and felt, briefly, like heat — and he understood that the operating theatre, the place that has defined his life, was no longer safe ground. He hopes to be able to work again without fear. What he is most afraid of is that the defect he senses in himself is permanent.
